items.text:
The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has finally opened, after 17 years of work put into its creation by George Lucas and his wife, businesswoman Mellody Hobson. While it has drawn large crowds from all walks of life, its proud founders have not forgotten that for many, particularly students and low-income families, museum pricing can be high, resulting in some missing out on a lunch or a treat during a visit. As such, they’ve implemented a few measures to keep it budget-friendly for everyone.
The inspiration behind this lies in Hobson’s personal story. While today she is president and co-CEO of Ariel Investments, and a former chair of both DreamWorks and Starbucks, Hobson grew up in poverty. Her mother, a single parent of six, struggled to make ends meet, sometimes not even having enough money to pay the rent. As a result of this financial challenge, Hobson often found herself unable to afford any food as a kid on a field trip at a museum. These experiences marked her profoundly. In fact, it prompted the couple to create affordable options for all visitors to their museum, where the lobby café offers $2 grilled cheese sandwiches. These simply yet satisfying sandwiches are made with American and cheddar cheese melted together between slices of buttered Pullman bread.
“That was the directive from the founders, George and Mellody,” Katie Harel, the restaurant’s managing director, told Forbes , “who were adamant that there would be something affordable in the café for everyone. So everyone can eat something in the café for $2. Every single person.” In addition to the grilled cheese option, the museum café also offers a $3 peanut butter and jelly sandwich.
Since no museum visit is complete without a trip to the gift shop, the Lucas Museum also offers some affordable souvenirs. The on-site shop sells 25¢ pencils listed as the Mellody Pencil . Part of the First Draft Collection , the stylish pencils include cheeky markings indicating how much of the pencil it would take to write a first, second, third, and final draft. The museum also offers a large selection of postcards for $2 each.
To plan your visit and book tickets, check out the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art website. To stay up to date with the museum, you can follow the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art on Instagram .

“Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
One can only imagine the pause, double-take, or request for clarity which followed this comment, made by a woman’s elderly aunt in the midst of an effort to clean out her East Village apartment.
Yet as the woman, who revealed herself only as Betsy, rummaged around in that closet 4 years later, she found an oil painting of undulating hills, with soft earthen colors reminiscent of the female form, which is now known to be Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, painted by the Mother of Modernism in 1930.
Its rediscovery has been hailed as “a once-in-a-lifetime moment, and absolutely thrilling.”
Soon to be auctioned at Christie’s where it’s expected to garner around $3 million, the story of its provenance first broke at the New York Post , who talked to Betsy about the fateful closet-cleaning
Her aunt, she said, was an “extremely intelligent” former foreign service member who had received the painting from Georgia O’Keeffe’s Manhattan art dealer in 1963 as a graduation present from her parents. At the time time it cost $3,800.
Her aunt loved the painting, and hung it in the apartment for years. It ended up in the closet after she noticed that an evening during a bridge game, one of the players kept his eyes fixed on it for far too long.
“I think she was fully aware of its value … she recognized that it was an expression of her financial position,” Betsy told the Post.
She decided to take it down so as to not draw attention to herself during similar soirées. Amid her fur coats the painting sat, even after her niece came over in 2022 to help clean out the apartment as the woman prepared to enter hospice care. It was only after her aunt passed away that Betsy followed up on the comment of the “O’Keeffe in the closet” that she found it, still in its original box marked “The Downtown Gallery, 51st St.”

items.title: Art trail celebrates arrival of black bears at zoo
items.desc: Jersey Zoo says the art trail will celebrate the world's "largest inhabitants to its smallest.
items.text:
Sculptures of bears and bees will be displayed across Jersey
A new public art trail will mark the arrival of Asiatic black bears, Jersey Zoo has said.
Sculptures of bears and bees would be put up across the island's wild landscapes, coastal spots and urban spaces to celebrate the arrival of the new species in their new enclosure next year, said bosses.
They said the installation, which launches in July next year, aimed to shine a light on "connections that sustain the natural world, from its largest inhabitants to its smallest".
Artists will be invited to submit designs to turn the sculptures into "distinctive works of art" while schools and community groups will also be encouraged to participate.
It is hoped the sculptures will then be sold a fundraising auction at the end of the summer.
Rebecca Brewer, chief executive of Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, said: "We want everyone who connects with our work, whether at Jersey Zoo or through our conservation projects around the world, to feel they can make a difference for nature.
"Our public art trails are a wonderful way to bring that belief to life."
Jersey Zoo will welcome Asiatic black bears in 2027
She said previous Go Wild Gorillas and Tortoise Takeover trails "brought so much joy to Jersey, encouraging people to explore parts of the island they might never have visited, walk new paths, meet new people and create lasting memories".
An auction of the 54 tortoise sculptures raised £720,000 for a new tropical house.

items.title: Duchy tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
items.desc: A ten-year strategy to raise £500m from the Duchy of Cornwall will see farms sold off across England.
items.text:
Plans to sell land and farms in Devon had already caused upset among tenants on the Duchy estate
Plans by the Prince of Wales to sell off up to 20% of the Duchy of Cornwall could see more tenant farmers across England asked to buy their farms or move out.
Up to 40 farm holdings across Devon, Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands could be affected by the sale, according to the Tenant Farmers Association (TFA).
Locals say talks over the future of nine farms on the Bradninch estate in Devon have already caused "distress" for some tenants who fear they cannot afford to buy.
A spokeswoman said the Duchy could not confirm the total number of tenants affected by the ten-year sale plan , external but told the BBC the estate was "supporting them through the process with care and respect".
The Duchy's rural director Matthew Morris said he was listening to feedback from farmers
The Duchy, which covers around 51,800 hectares (128,000 acres) in 19 counties, plans to use the £500m raised from the property and land sale over the next decade to invest in local communities, affordable housing and environmental projects.
Former GP Mary Ryan, a local Lib Dem councillor who has lived near the Bradninch estate for around 35 years and is supporting the farmers, said some of those affected were "experiencing enormous mental and emotional distress" as a result of the planned sell-off.
She added that while the Duchy had reportedly apologised to tenants last month, the handling of the process had been "pretty dire".
The sales programme has now been extended from Bradninch, near Cullompton, to the Duloe Estate in Cornwall and to individual holdings elsewhere in Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands, according to the TFA.
The Duchy's rural director, Matthew Morris, told the BBC he was listening to feedback over how the sales were being handled and offering support and mental health advice to tenants.
Morris added that the Duchy was "still committed to agriculture" but that there "may well be other disposals in the future".
In terms of immediate evictions, he said, there were "no cliff edges here" and that the Duchy was working closely with every tenant to find a suitable outcome.
"In the main, our mission is to sell to our farmers. We are keen that wherever possible we can achieve that continuity," Morris explained.

items.desc: Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Characters Come to Life in Major New York Exhibition Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara is bringing his instantly recognizable characters back to New York with a major exhibition at David Zwirner. Spanning two of the gallery’s Chelsea locations, the presentation features nearly 100 works, including new paintings, drawings, recent sculptures, and selections from earlier decades
items.text:
Installation view, Yoshitomo Nara, David Zwirner, New York, November 5—December 12, 2026.
Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara is bringing his instantly recognizable characters back to New York with a major exhibition at David Zwirner. Spanning two of the gallery’s Chelsea locations, the presentation features nearly 100 works, including new paintings, drawings, recent sculptures, and selections from earlier decades. It marks Nara’s first solo exhibition with David Zwirner and his first major solo presentation in New York in nearly a decade.
Best known for his oversized, wide-eyed figures, Nara has developed a visual language that balances playful imagery with a rebellious edge. His young-looking subjects often appear innocent at first glance, but their expressions suggest something more complicated. Some stare directly at the viewer with quiet defiance, while others carry an unmistakable sense of melancholy. Beneath their cartoonlike appearance, Nara’s characters confront ideas about childhood, vulnerability, resistance, and the realities of the world around them.
The exhibition also traces the development of Nara’s distinctive style. Earlier works from the late 1980s and 1990s appear alongside new pieces, offering a closer look at how his imagery has evolved. His latest paintings introduce muted colors and layered surfaces, while large-scale monochromatic drawings made with industrial paint sticks reveal the expressive energy of his drawing practice.
At the gallery’s 19th Street location, 13 monumental bronze sculptures transform the space. Coated in matte white, the oversized heads recall the snow-covered forests near Mount Hakkōda in northern Japan, where Nara grew up. Their imposing scale contrasts with their softly illuminated surfaces, creating an atmosphere of stillness. Together, the sculptures connect his familiar characters to the natural landscapes and childhood memories that continue to inform his work.
Yoshitomo Nara is on view at David Zwirner’s galleries at 533 West 19th Street and 537 West 20th Street in New York City from November 5 through December 12, 2026. Visit David Zwirner for additional information and exhibition details.

46 years ago today, NASA’s Voyager 1 probe arrived at Saturn and beamed back the first images ever taken of its rings. It arrived at our solar system’s second-largest planet via a gravitational assist trajectory at Jupiter which was replicated with Voyager 2. On November 12th, when the space probe came within 77,000 miles of Saturn’s cloud-tops, the space probe’s cameras detected complex structures in the rings of Saturn, and its remote sensing instruments studied the atmospheres of Saturn and its giant moon Titan. READ what it discovered… (1980)
Voyager 1 found that about 7% of the volume of Saturn’s upper atmosphere is helium (compared with 11% of Jupiter’s atmosphere), while almost all the rest is hydrogen. Since Saturn’s internal helium abundance was expected to be the same as Jupiter’s and the Sun’s, the lower abundance of helium in the upper atmosphere may imply that the heavier helium may be slowly sinking through Saturn’s hydrogen; that might explain the excess heat that Saturn radiates over energy it receives from the Sun.
Winds blow at high speeds on Saturn. Near the equator, the Voyagers measured winds about 500 m/s (1,100 mph). The wind blows mostly in an easterly direction. Voyager measured the rotation of Saturn (the length of a day) at 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds, and identified polar aurorae, and aurora-like ultraviolet emissions at middle latitudes. These remain a puzzle to this day, since bombardment by electrons and ions, known to cause auroras on Earth, occurs only at the high latitudes.

Pop culture knows of Maal likely through his provision of the music for Marvel’s Black Panther, but Maal has worked with artists as varied as Mumford & Sons, Taj Mahal, and Peter Gabriel.
Born in Podor, he helped his father, the muzzein at the local mosque, to perform the calls to prayer, which led to him developing an extremely resonant voice that rarely needed amplification. items.title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons after her home was destroyed and died before she could return
items.desc: Jean Powell kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow burst its banks.
items.text:
Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago
When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.
Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales last November.
But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.
"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."
The BBC report from November 2025 when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia
Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of November 15 last year as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.
It has been officially described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in Monmouth during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.
Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.
"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms most days.
"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."

"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."

items.title: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
items.desc: More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded at overflow sites previously unmonitored by Scottish Water, BBC Scotland News analysis has found.
items.text:
More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.
The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.
Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.
Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.
BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.
Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.
They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.
These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.
The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.
Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.
More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year – an average of about 274 a day.
It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.
The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.
Scottish Water figures , external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.
When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.

items.text:
Mexico City is a city of flowers. Around the Day of the Dead, the main avenues are painted orange with thousands upon thousands of marigolds, which later make way for red poinsettias as Christmas time arrives. And come spring, the jacaranda trees cover the ground with lilac-hued blooms. As such, the Mexican capital is the perfect spot for artist Cj Hendry to open a pop-up of her Flower Shop, offering her colorful plush blooms that blend art, design, and collectibles.
From Nov. 21 to 29, Cj Hendry’s Flower Shop will operate in the bustling Roma Norte neighborhood. The pop-up will feature a carefully curated collection of plush flowers, including a special selection of blooms that reflects the personality and energy of the host city. The organizers say the flowers will be priced at 150 pesos each (about $8). With every purchase of nine flowers, guests will receive a complimentary 10th one.
The Mexico City pop-up is part of a larger Flower Shop international tour, following the opening of permanent Flower Markets in New York and Hong Kong. After this stop, the plush blooms will make their way to Miami, Denver, London, Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane, and Perth.
“Flower Market began as an effort to unite communities around a universally shared joy: flowers,” says Hendry via a statement. “By expanding into Flower Shop, the goal was to share that experience globally, allowing people across various cities to engage with and gather these tactile creations. Each locale possesses a distinct atmosphere, and I am thrilled that every temporary installation will feature unique floral variations, distinctive surprises, and a tailored narrative.”
The Mexico City pop-up will be located at Mérida 87, Roma Norte, taking place Nov. 21-29 and open every day between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. There is also no need to go on the very first day of the event. According to the organizers, the flowers will be restocked every single day.

items.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
items.desc: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.
items.text:
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image)
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

items.text:
“He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail.” That’s how one rescuer in Kentucky described the moment he spotted 6-year-old Roman Heilman, a boy with autism missing for 3 days.
Jacob Mullins, a member of a local horse trailriding group, told the Lexington Herald Leader that he was only about a half-mile from Heilman’s home when he suddenly climbed out of a bush followed by a small dog, and and sang “Old McDonald.”
Heilman then grabbed onto the leg of the lead rescuer and didn’t want to let go.
He had been reported missing in the late afternoon on Sunday, November 1st, and the volunteers had been out since first light on Tuesday, looking around the wooded and mountainous area for hours, covering some 14 miles.
1 of 10 members of a horse trailriding group who live either side of the Kentucky-West Virginia state line, Jacob Mullins told the Lexington Herald Leader about the moment that the hunters became the hunted.
“We found him probably about a mile and a half from his house. He came out of the bushes saying ‘E-I-E-I-O horsey.’ He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail,” Mullins remembered.
“He was naked, and he was scratched, and he had a little dog with him. He ate a banana and drank some water and then we brought him off the hill.”
Roman is autistic, and when it was reported to police that he had wandered away from his house into the woods, “hundreds” volunteered to aid in the search. This included other teams on horseback, drones, but also motor vehicles, which Mullins thought perhaps had scared the boy from being found earlier.
Rescue authorities had received information on Sunday that the child had removed his clothing at some point, making the situation even more concerning. Indeed, he would have spent two frigid nights in the woods.
Travis Hughes, Director of Lawrence County Emergency Management, put out a heartfelt statement following the rescue on Facebook, in which he said he had “never been more proud” of the community.

“I have always said that when something happens here in Lawrence County, our people come together. But what I witnessed during this search was truly something special.”

items.title: The Handwritten Final Draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' Speech Was Considered Lost. It Turned Out to Be Sitting in a Desk Drawer for Decades
items.desc: Across seven yellow notepad pages, King is seen wrestling with word choice and revising his remarks the night before the March on Washington. The manuscript will head to auction in January and is expected to pull in more than $10 million
items.text:
It was late on August 27, 1963, and Martin Luther King Jr. was huddled with a group of his closest advisors in the lobby of the Willard Hotel in Washington, D.C.
They were drafting King’s closing remarks for the March on Washington , officially the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, which was set to start in just 12 hours. The group went back and forth on the message: Should it be ideological or Biblical? Directed towards the students marching or the nation at large?
As the night wore on, King eventually bowed out. “Okay brothers,” Clarence B. Jones , an activist and speechwriter for King, recalled him saying. “Thank you so much everybody for your suggestions and input … I am now going upstairs to my room to counsel with my Lord.”
Alone in his suite, King stayed up until 4 a.m., writing and revising his remarks on a yellow notepad, scratching out swaths of text in blue ink. He then sent these marked-up pages to be typed, forming the basis of his canonical “I Have a Dream” speech , delivered to more than 250,000 demonstrators gathered by the Lincoln Memorial .
Scholars have long assumed that the original, handwritten final draft had been discarded amid the day’s chaos. But six decades later, the manuscript has resurfaced from a drawer of one of King’s former aides. The seven yellow pages are set to be auctioned at Christie’s in January, where the draft is expected to sell for more than $10 million.
“When I first saw these pages and realized what they were, I was astounded,” Christie’s manuscripts specialist Peter Klarnet says in a statement . “This is a treasure of American history … Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time.”
Civil rights leader and philanthropist Xernona Clayton found the pages in the late 1990s. They were tucked in an envelope labeled “speech,” nestled among other papers in a desk drawer belonging to her late husband, Edward , one of King’s aides and speechwriters.
Clayton knew it was an important document related to the “I Have a Dream” speech but not that it was the final manuscript. She tucked it back in the desk drawer, not wanting to disrespect King’s memory by selling or displaying his memorabilia.
But in recent years, she changed her mind. “Now that I’m older, I’m wiser,” Clayton, now 96, tells the New York Times ’ Jennifer Schuessler. “It just seems like something that important ought to be shared.”

items.text:
Just a few weeks ago it was the driest place on Earth. Now it’s the most colorful.
Chile’s Atacama Desert has erupted into perhaps the greatest floral display ever recorded there, with some 200 species blooming—some in areas where flowers haven’t been seen since the before new millennium.
VIDEO: 🇨🇱 Chile's Atacama Desert fills with flowers in spring The phenomenon, known as the "flowering desert," occurs in certain years when rainfall and temperatures coincide, awakening the desert's dormant seeds #AFPVertical https://t.co/Cr4C3LaFa8
It means that seeds and tubers have lain dormant under the sand waiting for the lifegiving touch of water for decades—a remarkable adaptation. For the people who protect this desert ecosystem, it’s another reminder of the incredible resilience and diversity of life that makes this place worth protecting.
“This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains,” Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park in the Atacama, told NPR, whose images of the flowering have to be seen to be believed.
“But it’s a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months.”
This year’s Super El Niño weather event dumped record rainfall onto the landscape. Through July and August, flooding allowed water to permeate deep into the soil, touching seeds that normally escape seasonal rains.
The resulting “superbloom,” to use the California term, is easily the widest-reaching and most vivid in 30 years. It’s a record that might not stand for long though, as the world’s driest, non-polar desert is seeing more rainfall than usual.
NPR says the increased frequency of the seasonal rains are creating conditions for more varied animal life—albeit transiently—such as reptiles, insects, bats and other pollinators, and even larger animals like the iconic guanaco, a relative of the lama.

The Atacama is also host to one of South America’s largest botanical storehouses: the Initihuasi Seed Bank. This genetic mothership is the central node in a nationwide network of institutions that are safeguarding the country’s plant diversity, come what may, and its scientists aren’t wasting this opportunity to merely take photographs.

items.text:
The third-largest collection of Ice Age-era engravings ever found on Spain’s Mediterranean side was sitting in plain sight where visitors for centuries had been walking right by them.
“For more than six decades, thousands of visitors passed directly in front of the engraved surfaces, and in some cases inscribed names and dates over them, without the Paleolithic origin of the figures being recognized,” said Josep Maria Vergès, a researcher now working to reveal the origins of these cave works.
A statement on the discovery details that people have been visiting the cave, called Cova de la Font Major, in Catalonia since the 12th century.
From 1957 onwards it was widely frequented by visitors, spelunkers, and treasure hunters and it was even converted into a tourist attraction with a museum in 1993.
Having now seen what was “under their noses” the whole time, researchers couldn’t stop thinking how inconceivable it was that the countless visitors who came before had failed to see these carvings.
Located around 250 yards from the entrance, Vergès, and his co-author of a study presenting the discovery published in Antiquity , state that Font Major cave had long been assumed to be unsuitable for cave art because of the irregularity in shape and color of its walls.
Scientifically, the discovery is a major one.
The Iberian Peninsula contains over 50% of all cave art documented in Upper Paleolithic Europe, but its distribution is incredibly uneven. High concentrations are found between modern France and the Spanish region of Cantabria, but only 2 representations have ever been found in the entirety of Catalonia.
So its location bucks a trend; as does the quantity of carvings. From the Pyrenees to Gibraltar, around 75% of known Spanish cave art sites contain 5 depictions or fewer, and over 90% contain 20 or fewer.
In extreme contrast, Font Major contains 280, among which 55 separate animals are documented, including horses, wild oxen, bears, goats, and deer—”a transformational discovery” for the understanding of Paleolithic European art, the statement read.
In their study, the researchers detail that radiocarbon dating of organic elements in the cave shows human occupation going back as far as 40,000 BCE, and continuing right up to the Bronze Age.

items.text:
Watching adults misunderstand the cues of his autistic cousin, a teen taught himself machine learning to build technology that could help them.
His solution has more than 700 users in 12 countries, reaching families through autism therapy centers—all while remaining free.
Kora, a free app that helps parents and caregivers read the emotional cues of autistic children. The app will offer several possible readings of what an autistic child may be feeling without any scores, diagnoses, or judgements.
The story begins with the younger cousin of New Jersey high schooler Shashank Madala, who would on occasion get upset at family gatherings. The adults who loved him most would gather around and guess out loud about whether he was hungry or whether the room was too loud.
They were often wrong, Madala writes, and over time the boy stopped trying to tell them. Madala was just 15, with a single computer science class behind him, but nevertheless decided to take action.
Madala’s early versions of Kora gave caregivers one fast, confident answer, and he came to see that this repeated the very mistake his family had made with his cousin. He rebuilt the app to slow adults down, offering more than one possible reading and surfacing what it is least sure about.
The philosophy behind his work was that technology aimed at autistic children is often built to change the child. His aim was to flip that script.
“A tool that announces that a child is angry invites the adult to stop looking at the child,” he wrote in Autism Spectrum News in August.
A caregiver points a phone camera at the child, and Kora offers several possible readings of what the child may be feeling, with bars for happy, sad, angry, afraid, and neutral, along with suggestions for how to respond.
In a display of responsible use of AI beyond his years, Madala also programmed Kora to now flag when it is unsure, leaving the final judgment to the adult who knows the child.

The fruits of his labors won him major national award, and he’s since been recognized by Congress. In December 2025, Kora won first place in the Congressional App Challenge for New Jersey’s 10th Congressional District which included some 4,600 participants.
Kora was displayed in the US Capitol, and in 2026, a Joint Legislative Resolution of the New Jersey Senate and General Assembly lauded Madala for the victory.

items.text:
A viral moment from a doorbell camera that reached millions of people has now raised more than $76,000 to support a woman who spends her days caring for others.
When Suzanna Metcalf arrived at Pastor Neal Seiwert’s home in Castle Rock, Colorado last year, she apologized as she had mixed up their pizza order, and would have to return with the correct order. She blamed “getting old,” but the struggle on her face was clear.
Metcalf works delivery shifts while serving as the full-time caregiver for her 82-year-old mother, managing daily care, medical needs and household expenses.
Instead of frustration, Seiwert, his wife Hailee, and their three young daughters stepped outside, placed their hands on her shoulders, and prayed for her. The short clip, captured by a doorbell camera, showed Metcalf visibly moved by the unexpected kindness after a long day of work.
The video, posted by Seiwert, quickly went viral, with hundreds of commenters, who almost all had the same question: How can we help?
The Seiwerts found Metcalf, and with her permission, started a GoFundMe, which describes Suzanna as a woman who has spent years putting others first.
What began as a modest effort quickly grew. More than 2,600 donors have contributed over the last year, raising over $76,000 — far exceeding the initial $10,000 goal— to give Suzanna some financial breathing room as she continues caring for her mom.
Seiwert told the New York Post he wanted Metcalf to feel both his family’s support and a broader sense of being valued. “So many people are commenting on how it brought them to tears. There are many people who simply just need love,” he said.
A viral moment doesn’t change the demands of caregiving and delivery work. But it has shown, in concrete form, that one small pause for kindness can open the door for real help.

items.text:
The beloved glowworm has gotten a glow-up thanks to pro bono work by local conservationists.
Local wildlife enthusiast Peter Cooper collects and breeds glowworms in his spare time in a garden shed before releasing their larvae into a reserve in North Yorkshire where they haven’t been seen in 100 years.
The reserve’s manager credited Cooper’s “raw passion and enthusiasm” for relighting these fairy lamps after so long an absence.
Nosterfield Nature Reserve is described as “one of North Yorkshire’s most important wetland wildlife sites.”
It stretches around 600 acres across old limestone quarries that were sometimes naturally reclaimed and sometimes rewilded by the nonprofit Lower Ure Conservation Trust into a special habitat ideal for members of the Lampyridae family of bioluminescent insects.
Described by the poet Edmund Bogg as appearing like “lamps lit by the hands of fairy folk,” the family contains the animals we call fireflies, lightning bugs, and glowworms.
The Guardian described them as having once been abundant across Britain. They’ve since gone dark across wide swaths of the island, and are extremely difficult to re-establish.
Yet Cooper and other dedicated volunteers referred to as “glow-getters” have slowly built an expertise in the delicate art of rearing larvae in captivity, which they’re now leveraging to brighten the Yorkshire weald.

“They are incredibly rare in the region and I can’t tell you how excited the volunteers have been about it,” Simon Warwick, manager of the Nosterfield reserve, told the Guardian.
Cooper has counted 1,900 larvae in his shed that are due for release at Nosterfield this year—part of an ongoing process that he says can’t be confirmed as successful until the wild-bred offspring of these shed larvae reach maturity and shine their own lights in the Yorkshire darkness sometime in 2030.

items.text:
GNN Voices is a new series of first-person pieces from people worth listening to: practitioners, researchers, teachers, and neighbors sharing what they’ve learned and how they see things.
My dad’s name was Kiran. In Sanskrit, it means “a ray of light.”
I wrote my book, Making Sense of Purpose , in his memory. His name is in the subtitle.
My dad found a way to walk with people without carrying them; he found a way to guide them without giving them directions; he held space, he held hands, he held space for their wants, needs and expectations, and then he shined a light on what made them and mattered to them and what’s forward …
This week is Diwali, the festival of lights. This year, I want to make it a gift to everyone. A week to shine a light back on the year and move forward with purpose before we rush into the new one.
Wanting to avoid a doom scroll is hard. But giving people something to do instead maybe helps.
It happens more because of the environment we built than because of any flaw in us. We grab what fills us without considering whether it nourishes us.
A few minutes of reflection pays us back. Researchers at Harvard Business School found that new employees who spent the last 15 minutes of each training day writing and reflecting on what they’d learned performed 22.8% better on their final test.
Ten questions. Five days. One in the morning, one at night. A few minutes each. Write it down, or just reflect and take note. Either way counts.
We’re bad at knowing what will make us happy. We rarely get explicit about what made a good moment good. So we never ask people what made them happy; we ask what makes them smile as they reflect.
We are strengths to be harnessed. Not weaknesses to be fixed. And our values are who we are when the world is at its messiest. Kennon Sheldon and Andrew Elliot found that when our goals come from our values, we put in more sustained effort and are more likely to reach them.
Not every plateau needs to be broken. Self-forgiveness is the single most powerful action, wholly within your control, that allows you to empty your backpack. When we forgive ourselves, the likelihood going forward is that we’ll be faster to break free than if we carry the guilt forward. And big wins are made by small steps.
As David McRaney puts it, Anxiety = Fear + Uncertainty. Sorting what we can control, what we can influence and what is outside our control makes uncertainty feel less overwhelming. And compassion is about caring, not carrying.
Tash

items.title: Even Replacing Some of Your Dietary Dairy With Plant-Based Alternatives Can Lead to Nutrient Deficiencies, Study Suggests
items.desc: More people are swapping animal products with vegan milks, yogurts and cheeses, so scientists wanted to investigate the potential public health effects. Their findings hint that consumers should look for items with extra nutrients added, called fortified foods
items.text:
Alternative dairy products are widely available in many countries. Grocery stores and cafes frequently offer “milks” made from soy, almond, oat, rice or other crops. That’s good news for people who don’t consume dairy, as well as for our planet, since the production of plant-based milk is more environmentally friendly than regular milk.
But relying on these plant-based alternatives—even partially—might carry health risks. In a study published in the September issue of the journal Lancet Planetary Health , researchers ran computer simulations based on United Kingdom nutrition data and found that swapping standard dairy for vegan versions can lead to deficiencies of four vital nutrients. However, that could be combated by mandating that nutrients be added to plant-based dairy alternatives, as well as bread, making them fortified foods .
Vegan milks, cheeses, yogurts, ice creams and more are becoming increasingly popular as people turn to them for health or sustainability reasons. However, they often lack certain nutrients found in dairy.
To explore the potential public health implications, researchers pulled data from the U.K.’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey involving more than 3,500 people between the ages of 1.5 and 100 years old. They put that information into a computer model to simulate how swapping out regular milk, yogurt and cheese with commercially available plant-based versions affected intake of four micronutrients: iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12.
The results weren’t great. Even replacing a modest amount of dairy caused a decline in intake of all analyzed micronutrients. Iodine took the biggest hit. Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make certain hormones, and it’s also crucial for brain development. The micronutrient is especially important for infants, adolescents and pregnant people.
The survey data revealed that 54 percent of girls ages 14 to 18 weren’t eating enough iodine. Replacing just 35 percent of dairy with plant-based alternatives would cause the deficiency to jump to 65 percent. Similarly, 32 percent of women ages 19 to 49 were iodine deficient at baseline, and it would rise to 42 percent after the same dairy swap.
If dairy intake was completely replaced, 80 percent of teenage girls and 72 percent of teenage boys would be iodine deficient, according to the computer simulations.

items.title: Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know
items.desc: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
items.text:
McKenzie Prillaman | Assistant Digital Editor, Science & Innovation
This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025.
Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis.
Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue.
“It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.”
Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places. The disease is more common in tropical and subtropical regions , where these biting insects thrive, than in temperate climates.
Around three in four infected people are asymptomatic or have mild flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, nausea and rash. Muscle and joint pain is another common symptom, which is why the disease is sometimes called “breakbone fever.” Symptoms usually appear within two weeks of being bitten by an infected mosquito and clear up after a week or two.
However, one in four dengue cases becomes severe. Those symptoms include extreme abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing and blood in vomit or stool, and anyone experiencing them should seek medical care. These signs often appear after the fever goes away, and people who have previously been infected are at a greater risk of severe dengue.
Individuals who recover from dengue can continue feeling fatigued for several weeks.
Although dengue vaccines exist , none are currently approved for use in the United States. They’re authorized in nations where the disease is more common, such as Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and Thailand.

items.title: Neolithic Cannibalism Wasn't an Act of Desperation. Almost 1,000 Skeletal Fragments From Caves in Southern Spain Show How Eating Human Flesh Was a Continual Practice
items.desc: More than five decades after hordes of prehistoric bones were unearthed from three caves in Granada, new forensic techniques show how communities continued to consume their dead across distinct cultural eras
items.text:
For generations, human cannibalism in prehistoric Europe was viewed as a desperate response to starvation. Now, a forensic re-examination of three prehistoric cave sites in southern Spain reveals that people ate human remains as a ritual for millennia, including after violent clashes or as a standard funeral rite.
Researchers analyzed 967 skeletal fragments representing at least 60 individuals recovered from the caves of Malalmuerzo , Carigüela and Majolicas in the province of Granada . Using high-resolution microscopy, machine learning and radiocarbon dating, the team discovered that these grisly feasts were not confined to a single crisis, such as war or starvation. Instead, they unfolded in “context-dependent episodes” between roughly 5300 B.C.E. and 3760 B.C.E., according to a recent study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
The bone assemblages were first excavated in the 1970s under the direction of Miguel C. Botella , a forensic anthropologist at the University of Granada. Fifty years later, Botella joined a multi-disciplinary team to subject the historical collection to modern forensic analysis.
“Returning to these materials with new tools has allowed us to address questions that were impossible to answer at the time,” lead author Palmira Saladié , an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, explains in a statement .
By scrutinizing butchery traces, impact fractures and tooth marks under the microscope, the researchers distinguished between injuries inflicted on fresh bone around the time of death and natural degradation that took place years later. The skeletons bore unmistakable hallmarks of systematic butchery: defleshing cut marks, bones split open to harvest marrow, crushed crania to extract brain tissue and bones rendered translucent from boiling.
Despite common processing methods, each cave documented a distinct social reality behind the cannibalistic practices. Remains from Malalmuerzo Cave—which coincidentally translates to “Bad Lunch,” Botella tells Joshua Rapp Learn of the New York Times —likely date to an episode of communal violence around 5000 B.C.E. There, 77 percent of the 714 recovered fragments displayed fractures, Historia National Geographic ’s Juan Pedro Chuet-Missé reported in September.

items.text:
A man who received nothing but hate mail for his Halloween hobby proved to be just the treat that Tammy Wyche needed to brighten her weekly drive to cancer treatment appointments.
Though a front yard covered in skeletons might serve to remind someone of their mortality, Wyche marveled at the creativity with which the homeowner arranged his decorations.
Some were raising the flag at Iwo Jima, while another was giving its dog a bone. There was a bony beekeeper who stood behind a cowboy riding an osseous equine, not far from where two boneheaded tourists were taking a selfie.
Yet despite this macabre menagerie, the scariest thing to Mr. Bill Pyle was what tended to show up in his Oxford, Ohio mailbox in those weeks leading up to Halloween—accusations of devil worship, promises of his expedient arrival in hell, and other such condemnations.
This carried on year after year, until one fateful day when Pyle opened a letter that he said stopped him “dead in his tracks.”
“I have been driving past your house daily for the past 19 days on my way to radiation treatments. A highlight of my journey has been checking to see who else has joined the bone family & what they are up to,” Wyche wrote in a heartfelt, handwritten correspondence.
“Thankfully, Wed. Sept 11th is my final radiation treatment, though I may need to continue to drive by once in a while to see what’s new. Thanks for the diversion.”
“Tears came to my eyes,” Pyle told CBS News’ ‘On the Road’ with Steve Hartman, remembering when he read it the first time. “[It]really touched my heart.”
Seeing the date of her final treatment, Pyle decided to roll the bones on a big surprise for this special admirer.
When Wyche drove past the ‘Bone Family’ that Wednesday morning, she looked to the right and saw a whole skeleton crew cheering her on with signs that celebrated this final milestone.
“It was very touching to think that somebody would go to that effort for a stranger,” she said.
Thanks to the story of Wyche’s brush with death at Pyle’s house, for every one person that has a bone to pick with him, there are 30—from as far away as Australia—sending messages of appreciation that encourage him to keep going with his skeletons.

Photographer of the Year, First place: Cultural, Historic & Heritage, Open Color, Honorable mention: Fine Art Rows of empty seats sit beneath tiers of ornate boxes inside an Italian theatre dating from the eighteenth century. Alessia Santambrogio’s central viewpoint brings the painted ceiling and the auditorium into a single view. Warm lighting reveals the repeated balconies without losing the room’s overall shape.
A small shift in perspective can completely transform the way something looks. This seems especially true in architectural photography. A sprawling building can suddenly feel intimate in a closely cropped shot of an alcove, while wood can look lyrical thanks to the composition’s sweeping curves. Brilliant architecture sits at the intersection of design and artistry, and a new photo contest recognizes the images that make structures shine, both on grand and granular scales. The 2026 PERSPA Awards recently shared its winning images from Architectural Perspective, the prize’s inaugural season.
The PERSPA Awards honor images of the built environment, showcasing historic and contemporary structures through categories including Stairs, Modern Architecture, Cultural, Geometry, and Human and Architecture. It also crowns a Photographer of the Year, with Alessia Santambrogio being the first person to win the top prize for her series depicting an 18th-century Italian theater.
Santambrogio chose to focus on the grandeur of the architecture. No patrons sit in the seats, making the interior’s beauty our sole focus. Santambrogio, whose background is in opera photography, captures a singular view from the stage, taking in the ornate boxes lining the theater, its illuminated archways, the striking ceiling with a large painting and the modeled flourishes surrounding it. At once, the image highlights how function and beauty aren’t mutually exclusive. Here, the grandeur complements the live artistry on stage.

items.title: The Maya Loved Using Mercury-Rich Red Paint to Decorate Pottery, Temple Walls and Even Burials. They May Have Accidentally Poisoned Their Own Water and Food Supply in the Process
items.desc: Testing of ancient sediment from two lakes in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula has revealed "crazy" high concentrations of mercury, as one researcher puts it, confirming findings from other regions of the Mesoamerican civilization
items.text:
The Maya loved cinnabar , a bright red ore used to decorate pottery, burial sites, structures and more. But cinnabar is roughly 86 percent mercury , a highly toxic element that can harm humans, animals and ecosystems.
The Maya used so much of this prized pigment that they polluted some of their cities. Now, new research suggests the Maya’s cinnabar-derived mercury contamination was even more widespread than previously thought—and it could have contributed to the civilization’s downfall.
Testing of ancient sediment from two lakes in modern-day Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula has revealed high concentrations of mercury during ancient Maya occupation. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Science Advances , suggest mercury pollution took a toll on the lakes’ aquatic ecosystems, causing their populations of aquatic creatures to decline or collapse. If the Maya ate fish or drank water from the lakes, they could have been exposed to toxic concentrations of mercury for decades or even centuries.

Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science
Matthew Holman , a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.
Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”
Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić . They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.
“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks , he says.
The object, called 2026 ED138 , is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.
“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne , a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”
Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides . items.desc: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, one expert says.
items.text:
Lydia Dibben wants more small farms around Wales growing produce
Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , external , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture , external , only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture , external .
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.
"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher.
Food security has become a hot topic , with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber-attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."
Duncan Fisher said he has hope that Wales will be able to increase its fruit and veg growing
Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.
They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.
As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.
"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."
But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.

items.desc: Recently obtained by the Library of Congress, the 1760 letter offers positive news about the health of four-year-old Martha Parke Custis, known as Patsy, the stepdaughter of George Washington
items.text:
More than 260 years ago, Martha Washington wrote to a friend with encouraging news about her young daughter’s health. Now, that letter has found a new home at the Library of Congress, offering a rare glimpse into the family’s private life.
Martha penned the note on September 29, 1760. Writing to Margaret Bolan Green, she provided an update on her four-year-old daughter “Patsy.”
“I have the pleasure to tell you my dear little girl is much better,” she wrote. “She has lost her fitts & fevours bout and seems to be getting well very fast.”
The Library of Congress purchased the letter for $47,500 in June during a Heritage Auctions sale, with funding from the James Madison Council’s Edwin L. Cox Legacy Trust, a permanent endowment that helps the library acquire materials. The library already had 11 of Martha’s letters, but this is the first that bears her handwriting.
“Very few of Martha Washington’s letters survive, as she appears to have destroyed most of her own private correspondence,” Elizabeth Novara , the American women’s history specialist for the library’s Manuscript Division, writes in a blog post . “Even brief documentation of her relationships with family and friends, as may be found in this letter, is important to understanding women’s lives during this time period.”
“Patsy”—whose full name was Martha Parke Custis —was one of the four children Martha had with her first husband, Daniel Parke Custis . The two had been married for just seven years when Custis died from a sudden illness in July 1757, at the age of 45. Two years later, at age 27, the widowed Martha married George Washington. Together, they raised the two surviving children from Martha’s first marriage, Patsy and John “Jacky” Parke Custis . (The other two, Daniel Parke Custis and Frances Parke Custis, died while their father was still alive.).
Historians believe that William Costin , a prominent member of Washington, D.C.’s free Black community, was likely Martha Washington’s grandson —the child of her son from her first marriage, Jacky, and an enslaved woman.
Martha wrote the letter after George Washington had served as commander of the Virginia Regiment during the French and Indian War but before he had become the nation’s first president . Historians now suspect that Patsy’s “fitts & fevours” were symptoms of epilepsy , a neurological disorder caused by abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain. A 1763 map of Jamaica showing the island’s parishes, settlements, and geographical features. (Photo: Thomas Craskell, Henry Moore, James Simpson, and Daniel Fournier via Library of Congress , Public Domain )
Tracing your family tree can sometimes lead to unexpected discoveries, but for descendants of enslaved people, finding information about their ancestors can be especially difficult. Ancestry is hoping to make that process a little easier with the release of nearly 4 million records documenting enslaved individuals across 20 former British colonies. They span across the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Indian Ocean, and South Africa. They include places such as Jamaica, Barbados, the Bahamas, Trinidad, Mauritius, and South Africa.
Released on September 22, 2026, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers collection includes around 300,000 digitized pages dating from 1813 to 1840. For the first time, the records have been fully indexed and made searchable online, giving descendants across the African diaspora a new way to explore their family histories.
“For descendants of enslaved individuals, family history research may often present a set of unique challenges to overcome, but what makes this collection so groundbreaking is its extraordinary level of detail,” says Nicka Sewell-Smith, professional genealogist and Senior Story Producer at Ancestry. “Featuring names, ages, and family connections, these registers give descendants across the diaspora a real opportunity to solve longstanding family mysteries and speak their ancestors’ names back into history.”
The proclamation of the abolition of slavery in Jamaica in Spanish Town on August 1, 1838. (Photo: Thomas Ashburton Picken via Wikimedia Commons , Public Domain )
Depending on the individual record, researchers may find names, ages, genders, family relationships, physical descriptions, births, deaths, and even information about a person’s African origins before enslavement. Details like these can be especially valuable for people trying to trace family histories that were disrupted by slavery.
The registers themselves have a much darker origin. Following Britain’s abolition of the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, the government required colonies to document enslaved populations in an effort to prevent illegal trafficking. These records were ultimately created as part of a system that treated human beings as property and kept track of enslaved populations before emancipation.

Despite painting himself around 35 times, there is only one confirmed photographic portrait of Vincent van Gogh that clearly shows his face. Taken in 1873, when the artist was 19 years old, the photograph captures a young Van Gogh staring unsmilingly into the camera, as was common for portrait photography at the time.
Around the time the photograph was taken, Van Gogh was working in the art trade. It would still be several years before he decided to become an artist and began creating the paintings he is known for today.
Photo: Jacobus Marinus Wilhelmus de Louw via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
Over the years, several other photographs have been associated with Van Gogh, although most have never been authenticated. One image was believed for decades to show a 13-year-old Vincent. In 2018, however, researchers determined that the boy was actually his younger brother, Theo van Gogh, who was photographed in Brussels at age 15 in 1873.
Photo: Ernest Ladrey via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
The mistake is understandable. The brothers shared similar features, and the photograph had been accepted as an image of Vincent for more than 60 years. Once it was correctly identified, the 1873 portrait of 19-year-old Vincent once again became his only known photographic portrait.

Sometimes referred to as a photograph of “Brussels clergymen,” the image has never been authenticated as a portrait of the artist. The Canadian photographer’s information printed on the photograph also makes the identification unlikely, since Van Gogh never traveled outside Europe.

The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.
And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.
As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.
America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.
The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

On Sunday, November 8, hundreds of people gathered around Chicago’s iconic Cloud Gate sculpture (aka “The Bean”) with one unusual goal: moving it 7 inches to the left. It was quite an ambitious feat, considering the sculpture weighs about 110 tons. Although the crowd was ultimately unsuccessful, the humorous stunt brought Chicagoans together for an afternoon of fun.
The event began with flyers posted around Chicago that simply read, “We need to move the bean seven inches to the left,” with no further explanation. The flyers instructed people to gather at Millennium Park at exactly 12:47 p.m., and the unusual request quickly gained attention on social media.
The reason behind the stunt was an ongoing internet joke that claims a man is trapped inside the sculpture. According to an online invitation for the event, moving The Bean would supposedly reveal a hidden door, allowing people to give the imaginary man a pickle and other resources.
On the day of the event, hundreds of people showed up to participate, with videos showing crowds pushing against the sculpture in unison. Despite their combined efforts, The Bean didn’t budge.
Created by artist Anish Kapoor between 2004 and 2006, The Bean’s nickname comes from the sculpture’s unusual shape. Its 168 stainless steel plates are welded together and polished to create a seamless, mirror-like surface perfect for pictures and selfies. Over the years, it has become one of Chicago’s most recognizable landmarks.
Although the crowd couldn’t accomplish its original goal, the Millennium Park Foundation welcomed the playful gathering. Kathryn Deery, an executive director for the foundation, told People that the event was a creative way to bring people together and celebrate one of the city’s most famous landmarks.
The sculpture remained in place and received its usual cleaning afterward, leaving behind little more than extra handprints and a memorable afternoon for the people who participated.

items.desc: A new study reveals the step-by-step process some octopuses use to cram themselves into tight openings. The findings could inspire new designs for soft robots used during search-and-rescue missions
items.text:
Octopuses are talented escape artists, capable of squeezing their bodies through seemingly impenetrable gaps to avoid danger, find hidden prey or break out of captivity . Scientists have long wondered how these eight-limbed creatures manage such impressive feats of flexibility. Now, they say they have some answers.
A study published November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology describes the step-by-step processes some octopuses use to cram themselves into tight spaces. In addition to expanding our understanding of these crafty cephalopods, the findings could help engineers improve the design of soft robots that need to fit into small spaces, such as those used during search-and-rescue missions.
“You always just think as a biologist that this is a minor question: How to squeeze your body into a crevice, through a hole or into a cave,” study co-author Michael Kuba , a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, tells IFLScience ’s Rachael Funnell. “But working with soft robotic engineers, you realize that there is so much more to how they manage to do this. They have several steps of the movement, and they have specific postures and body parts they use to move through a hole.”
In the study, Kuba and colleagues conducted laboratory experiments involving three subadult common octopuses ( Octopus vulgaris ) and four juvenile Mayan octopuses ( O. maya ). The team started by measuring the distance between each animal’s eyes to determine the size of the semi-rigid cartilage casing surrounding their brains. Then, they adjusted a clear, acrylic tank partition to create a single, central hole that was either smaller or larger than the measurements, which ranged from about 0.4 to 1.4 inches. One at a time, they placed the octopuses in the tank, then watched and filmed what happened next.
“We know that they can squeeze through all these spaces, but nobody’s actually looked at how they do this,” study co-author Tamar Gutnick , a biologist at the Haus des Meeres-Aqua Terra Zoo in Austria, tells NPR ’s Ari Daniel. “So, what we did was take octopuses and systematically make them go through different-sized holes.”
Octopus bodies are mostly soft and pliable. These creatures have only two stiffer body parts: a cartilaginous shell that protects their brains and a beak —made of a hard material called chitin—that they use to eat.

Residents in King's Lynn are campaigning for more green space to be protected
After a successful campaign getting parkland protected, residents in a Norfolk town are asking for more space to be given the same safeguards from development.
Seven acres (2.8 hectares) of land known as Harding's Pits, beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, will be preserved after it was given "village green status" by the county council .
The Harding's Pits Community Association had campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as leisure space.
Next, the group wants the protection to be extended to the east side, which has been earmarked for up to 50 houses in King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council's local plan , external . The authority has been approached for comment.
The land in the foreground has been given protected status, but the space closer to the town centre at the top has been earmarked for housing
Alexandra Kemp, an independent councillor, said she was asking her authority to amend its local plan.
She said: "I want to protect the east side of Hardings Way as a village green. To take out the 50 houses earmarked for Harding's Pits east from the borough's local plan, and provide community sports facilities, more trees and places for wildlife instead.
"Any development along Hardings Way risks more general traffic which would be devastating to the peace, quiet, safety, and amenity and wildlife."
The local council has been given a target to build more than 10,000 new homes by 2040 by the government.
Harding's Pits is located alongside the River Great Ouse
Harding's Pits was turned into a public space in the early 1960s, but was originally a 19th Century clay pit which was then used as landfill.
The site is currently used for dog walking and as pedestrian access to King's Lynn town centre.

Seabed Thriving 10 Years After Scottish Dredging Ban
Islanders Celebrate Protections of Their Magical Maerl Beds
Fish Stocks Thrive Thanks to This Strange Seaweed and Locals Who Protected It
A ban on industrial scallop dredging has been “the most amazing thing to happen” to the residents, both man and marine, of the Summer Isles.
In place for 10 years, the ban has protected this extraordinary kind of magenta-colored seaweed called maerl, which forms hard, chalky nodules like coral on the seabed, and has allowed for whales, dolphins, porpoises, and key fish stocks to thrive.
Scallop dredging around the Summer Isles had damaged this incredible marine seascape for decades until a coalition of citizen scientists and activists got the activity banned inside a 150,000-acre protected area off the northwest coast of Scotland that contains all the area’s maerl beds, including 2 that are over a mile long which have been growing in the same place for 9,000 years.
Maerl builds up overtime into beds and carpets that interlock, creating magnificent marine habitat for fish species to breed.
Looking somewhat like the pieces from a game of knucklebones, the free movement of water between each nodule provides for excellent circulation which the foundational species of the marine food web need. They in turn provide for the species above and beyond them, all the way up to dolphins and humans.
The protections have been the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles,” one local activist and artist named Diyanna Ross told the Guardian. “It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”
The Blue Hope Alliance, of which Ross is a part, also includes an association of Scottish “creel” fishermen, a smaller, more sustainable method of harvesting seafood that doesn’t deplete underlying stocks.
Decades of dredging had severely depleted scallop numbers, requiring industrial fishing operations to damage more and more seabed in search of the bivalves.
The 10-year-old campaign to ban scallop dredging, the Guardian reports , was as much about allowing these creel fishermen to continue to harvest scallops as it was about allowing the scallop to recover.

A 103-year-old D-Day veteran was reunited with his war medals just in time for Remembrance Day.
The story came about through a remarkable coincidence when an amateur WWII historian came across the man’s military record and medals, and contacted the family wondering if he still had them.
“They may be just a piece of metal but the medals are something that I hold very close to my heart,” said veteran Douglas Halley, proudly wearing them on his sweater. “They remind me of all my brothers in arms who I was with who helped me get through in the war.”
Halley was just 20 when he landed on the Normandy beaches with the Royal Artillery in the second wave of troops, having been conscripted into the war out of the shop where he was training to be a butcher.
Born in England’s South Yorkshire, Halley was awarded 3 medals: the 1939-45 Star, the France and Germany Star, and the War Medal 1939-45.
He accidentally left them pinned to his uniform, which he returned at the end of the war in 1945—thus losing them exactly when they were the most prestigious of honors.
Last January, 27-year-old Joseph Smith contacted Halley’s grandson, Luke Halley, after seeing Luke’s Veterans Day (called Remembrance Day in the UK) Facebook post about his grandfather.
Smith has been travelling across the UK documenting veterans’ stories for a project titled, The Last of The Greats . He hopes to document as many veterans’ stories for the younger generation so they can learn about and remember their sacrifices.
SIMILAR STORIES TO THIS: Young Man Interviews 3,000 World War II Vets Over 10-year Project–Preserving Their Stories
It was for this project that Smith came across Halley and his medals, contacted Luke via Facebook, and asked if the veteran still had them. Learning about the accident with the uniform in 1945, Smith helped the Halley family contact the Ministry of Defense and fill out the necessary forms to have the medals returned.
“If I can help a veteran or their family in any way, be it getting hold of medals or finding out further information, it is the least I can do,” Smith told the Southwest News Service. “It is an honor, really.”
